orig_functions_inverse.description: Learn domain, range and inverse functions for Cambridge 9709 Pure 1. Follow a restricted graph, test whether a function is one–one and check your answers.

sections.title: What does f(x) tell me?
sections.label: Inputs and outputs
sections.intro: Put \(2\) into the rule \(f(x)=5-2x\). The result is \(1\), so \(f(2)=1\). Here \(2\) is the input and \(1\) is its output.

blocks.html:
A function gives exactly one output for each allowed input. The domain tells you what you may put in. The range tells you which values can come out.

The notation \(f:x\mapsto5-2x\) names the same rule. Read it as “\(f\) maps \(x\) to \(5-2x\)”.

If the same input were paired with both \(3\) and \(5\), the rule would give two answers for one input. That breaks the definition of a function.

blocks.prompt: The function \(g(x)=2-3x\) has domain \(-3\le x<1\). Find \(g(-2)\).
blocks.hint: Replace \(x\) with \((-2)\). What is \(-3\times(-2)\)?
blocks.solution: \(-2\) belongs to the domain, so \(g(-2)=2-3(-2)=8\).

retry.feedback: You used the effect of a positive input. Put the negative input in brackets: \(2-3(-2)\).
\(-2\) is the input. Substitute it into the rule to find the output.

sections.title: Which inputs are allowed?
sections.label: Find the domain
sections.intro: Start with any restriction stated in the question. Then keep only inputs for which the formula is defined over the real numbers.

blocks.html:
• For a square root, the expression inside the root must be at least zero.
  • For a fraction, its denominator must be non-zero.
  • When both rules apply, every allowed input must satisfy both.

blocks.prompt: Let \(k(x)=\dfrac{\sqrt{2-x}}{x+3}\), with \(x\ge-5\). Give the complete domain. You can use an interval union or join conditions with and.
blocks.hint: Find where \(2-x\ge0\) and \(x+3\ne0\). Combine these with \(x\ge-5\).
blocks.solution: The root requires \(x\le2\). The fraction excludes \(x=-3\). The complete domain is \(-5\le x\le2\) with \(x\ne-3\), or \([-5,-3)\cup(-3,2]\).

retry.feedback: Your outer boundaries are right. Remove \(x=-3\), where the denominator is zero.
You used both restrictions from the formula. Keep the given lower boundary \(x\ge-5\) as well.
Try the endpoint \(x=2\). A zero inside a square root is permitted, and the denominator is non-zero there.

sections.title: Which outputs does the graph reach?
sections.label: Read the range
sections.intro: Return to \(f(x)=5-2x\) with \(-2\le x<3\). Read the domain along the horizontal axis and the range along the vertical axis. The hollow point shows where the allowed line stops.

blocks.html: For a line segment, find the output at each boundary. Put the smaller output first, then decide which boundary outputs are included. A decreasing line sends the larger input to the smaller output.
Keep the bracket with its value when the order reverses. Here the excluded input is the upper boundary \(3\), but its output \(-1\) is the lower boundary of the range.

blocks.prompt: Find the range of \(g(x)=11-3x\), where \(-1<x\le3\). Give an inequality in \(g(x)\) or \(y\), or give an interval.
blocks.hint: Compare the outputs at \(x=-1\) and \(x=3\). Which input is actually included?
blocks.solution: The line approaches \(14\) as \(x\) approaches \(-1\), and reaches \(2\) at \(x=3\). So \(2\le g(x)<14\), or \([2,14)\).

retry.feedback: The output \(2\) comes from the included input \(3\). The output \(14\) would need the excluded input \(-1\).
You have listed the allowed inputs. Substitute both boundaries to find the output values.

sections.title: Can I always get back to one input?
sections.label: Test for one–one
sections.intro: Look at the output \(6\) on the graph of \(q(x)=(x-1)^2+2\). The full parabola reaches it at \(x=-1\) and \(x=3\). On \(x\ge1\), only the solid branch is allowed.

blocks.html: A one–one function uses each attained output once. On the allowed graph, every horizontal line must meet the curve at most once. One horizontal line through two points is enough to show a function is many–one.
In a many–one function, different inputs can share an output. Each input still has just one output. A vertical line tests that first rule. A horizontal line tests whether the rule is reversible.

blocks.prompt: The function \(r(x)=(x+2)^2+1\) has domain \(x\ge-3\). Give the two allowed inputs that produce \(2\). They show why \(r\) is many–one.
blocks.hint: Solve \((x+2)^2=1\) using both signs, then check the domain.
blocks.solution: \(x+2=\pm1\), so \(x=-3\) or \(x=-1\). Both are allowed and give output \(2\). The same output has two possible inputs.

retry.feedback: \(-1\) is on the right of the vertex. Use the negative square root to find the point on the left. The boundary \(x=-3\) is included.
\(-3\) is included. Use the other sign for \(x+2\) to find the second allowed input.

sections.title: What does the inverse do?
sections.label: Reverse the inputs and outputs
sections.intro: In our first example, \(f(2)=1\). If you give the output \(1\) to the inverse, it returns the input \(2\).

blocks.html: To reverse a one–one function, read every arrow backwards. The outputs of \(f\) become the allowed inputs of \(f^{-1}\). The inputs of \(f\) become the range of \(f^{-1}\).
Read \(f^{-1}\) as “\(f\) inverse”. It reverses the mapping. For our rule, \(f^{-1}(1)=2\), whereas the reciprocal \(\dfrac1{f(1)}=\dfrac13\).

blocks.prompt: For \(v(x)=3x-4\) on all real numbers, give \(v^{-1}(5)\).
blocks.hint: Ask which original input gives output \(5\). Solve \(3x-4=5\).

retry.feedback: \(\dfrac1{11}\) is the reciprocal of \(v(5)\). To use the inverse, start from output \(5\) and solve for the original input.
\(11\) is the result of putting \(5\) into \(v\). For the inverse, \(5\) is the original output. Which input produces it?

blocks.prompt: A function consists of \(-4\mapsto3\), \(-1\mapsto0\) and \(5\mapsto8\). Give all ordered pairs \((\text{input},\text{output})\) for its inverse.
blocks.hint: Reverse each pair. The new first coordinate must be an output of the original function.

retry.feedback: These are the original pairs. Reverse the coordinates within each pair to make the original output the new input.

sections.title: How do I find the inverse formula and its domain?
sections.label: Find an inverse rule
sections.intro: Finding an inverse is like solving for the starting number when you know the result. Use \(y\) to hold the original output while you rearrange.

blocks.title: Reverse the rule in four steps
blocks.html:
1. Check that the function is one–one on its stated domain.
  2. Write \(y=f(x)\) and solve for the original \(x\).
  3. Write the result in inverse notation. The old \(y\) is the input of the inverse, so rename it \(x\) in \(f^{-1}(x)\).
  4. Use the range of \(f\) as the domain of \(f^{-1}\).

When asked for the inverse and its domain, give the rule and the full interval. Check one known pair in both directions. The pair can catch a sign error, while the original range determines which inverse inputs are allowed.

blocks.prompt: For \(g(x)=10-4x\), with \(0<x\le2\), find \(g^{-1}(x)\). Enter the expression to the right of the equals sign.
blocks.hint: From \(y=10-4x\), first isolate \(4x\). Then divide by \(4\).
blocks.solution: \(4x=10-y\), so the old input is \(\dfrac{10-y}{4}\). The inverse rule is \(g^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{10-x}{4}\).

retry.feedback: When you add \(4x\) and subtract \(y\), you get \(4x=10-y\). Check the order of the terms in your numerator.

blocks.prompt: Now give the domain of \(g^{-1}\) for that same function \(g(x)=10-4x\), \(0<x\le2\).
blocks.hint: The original range becomes the inverse domain. Compare the outputs at \(x=0\) and \(x=2\).
blocks.solution: \(g(2)=2\), and \(g(x)\) approaches \(10\) as \(x\) approaches \(0\) from above. The inverse domain is \(2\le x<10\), or \([2,10)\).

retry.feedback: That is the domain of \(g\). Use the outputs of \(g\) as the inputs of the inverse.
The value \(10\) would come from the excluded original input \(0\), so the inverse cannot take \(10\).

sections.title: Where does an excluded value go when I reverse a fraction?
sections.label: Invert a fractional rule
sections.intro: An excluded input and a missing output are two different restrictions. On reversing the function, the missing output becomes the excluded input.

blocks.html: For a rule of the form \(b+\dfrac{a}{x-c}\), with \(a\ne0\) and \(x\ne c\), the fraction cannot be zero. The output cannot be \(b\). For every other output, solving for \(x\) gives exactly one permitted answer.

field.label: Numerator and denominator of the inverse

blocks.prompt: Find the inverse rule of \(s(x)=1+\dfrac6{x-4}\), \(x\ne4\). Enter it as one fraction, using a semicolon between the numerator and denominator.
blocks.hint: Make \(x-4\) the subject of \(y-1=\dfrac6{x-4}\). Then collect the terms over a single denominator.
blocks.solution: \(x=4+\dfrac6{y-1}\). Rename the input to get \(s^{-1}(x)=4+\dfrac6{x-1}=\dfrac{4x+2}{x-1}\). Enter 4x + 2 ; x − 1.

blocks.prompt: For the same function \(s\), state the complete domain of \(s^{-1}\). Give an inequality with \(\ne\) (you can type !=) or both intervals.
blocks.hint: Which value can \(1+\dfrac6{x-4}\) never produce?
blocks.solution: The missing original output is \(1\). The inverse domain is all real \(x\) with \(x\ne1\), or \((-\infty,1)\cup(1,\infty)\).

retry.feedback: \(4\) is excluded from the original inputs. The restriction on the inverse input comes from the missing original output, \(1\).
\(1\) is the value you must exclude. Use \(x\ne1\) or give the intervals on both sides of \(1\).

examples.title: Use the rule and its stated domain
examples.question: For \(f:x\mapsto 5-2x\), \(-2\le x<3\), find \(f(-2)\). Is \(f(3)\) defined?
solution:
The input \(-2\) is included. Substitute it into the rule.

\[f(-2)=5-2(-2)=9.\]
The input \(3\) is excluded by \(x<3\). The expression \(5-2x\) can be evaluated there, but \(f(3)\) is undefined on the stated domain.

examples.title: Combine the square root, denominator and stated limit
examples.question: Find the domain of \(h(x)=\dfrac{\sqrt{x+1}}{x-4}\), subject to \(x\le6\).
solution: The square root permits \(x+1\ge0\), so \(x\ge-1\). Together with \(x\le6\), this gives \([-1,6]\) before checking the denominator.
Remove \(4\) because it makes the denominator zero. At \(-1\), the numerator is zero and the denominator is non-zero, so that endpoint stays.
The domain is \(-1\le x\le6\) with \(x\ne4\), or \([-1,4)\cup(4,6]\).

examples.title: Keep the correct output endpoint
examples.question: Give the range of the line \(f(x)=5-2x\) on \(-2\le x<3\).
solution: The included input \(-2\) gives \(9\). The line decreases from there, so \(9\) is an attained maximum.
At the excluded boundary \(x=3\), the expression gives \(-1\). As the input approaches \(3\) from below, the output approaches \(-1\) from above. No other input gives \(-1\).
The line reaches every output in between. Write \(-1<f(x)\le9\), \(-1<y\le9\) or \((-1,9]\).

examples.title: The same parabola with two domains
examples.question: Decide whether \(q(x)=(x-1)^2+2\) is one–one on all real inputs and then on \(x\ge1\).
solution: On all real inputs, \(q(-1)=q(3)=6\). Starting from \(6\), you cannot tell which input was used. The full parabola is many–one.
On \(x\ge1\), the distance \(x-1\) from the vertex increases with \(x\). Its square increases too, so every attained output comes from just one input.
Both domains give the range \([2,\infty)\), but only the restricted domain here gives a one–one function.

examples.title: Reverse every mapping in a finite set
examples.question: A function \(m\) has the three mappings \(-3\mapsto2\), \(0\mapsto4\) and \(2\mapsto7\). Describe its inverse.
solution: The outputs \(2\), \(4\) and \(7\) are distinct. Starting from any one of them, there is a unique way back.
Reverse each arrow. The inverse is \(2\mapsto-3\), \(4\mapsto0\) and \(7\mapsto2\).
The inverse domain is \(\{2,4,7\}\). Its range is \(\{-3,0,2\}\).

examples.title: Undo the decreasing rule
examples.question: Find \(f^{-1}(x)\) and its domain when \(f(x)=5-2x\) and \(-2\le x<3\).
solution:
The line is strictly decreasing, so it is one–one. Let \(y=5-2x\) and make the old input \(x\) the subject.

\[2x=5-y,\qquad x=\frac{5-y}{2}.\]

The old output \(y\) is the new input. Write it as \(x\) in inverse notation.

\[f^{-1}(x)=\frac{5-x}{2}.\]
The original range was \((-1,9]\), so the inverse takes \(-1<x\le9\). Its outputs satisfy \(-2\le y<3\), the original input restriction.
Check the pair from the beginning. Since \(f(2)=1\), the inverse should return \(2\). In fact \(f^{-1}(1)=\dfrac{5-1}{2}=2\).

examples.title: Keep track of both exclusions
examples.question: Find the inverse of \(p(x)=3+\dfrac4{x+2}\), with \(x\ne-2\). State its domain and range.
solution: Write \(y-3=\dfrac4{x+2}\). The right-hand side is never zero, so \(y\ne3\).

For each \(y\ne3\), solve for exactly one old input.

\[x+2=\frac4{y-3},\qquad x=\frac4{y-3}-2.\]

Rename the input of the inverse.

\[p^{-1}(x)=\frac4{x-3}-2,\qquad x\ne3.\]
The inverse output is never \(-2\). Its range is \(y\ne-2\), the set of original inputs.

glossary.definition: A rule that gives exactly one output for each allowed input.
All allowed inputs. Read them on the \(x\)-axis.
All outputs actually reached. Read them on the \(y\)-axis.
Each output in the range comes from just one input.
The rule \(f^{-1}\) that takes an original output back to its unique input.

revision.body:
Read the function

The domain is the set of allowed inputs. The range is the set of outputs reached on that domain. Check stated restrictions, denominators and square roots before substituting.

For \(f(x)=5-2x\) on \(-2\le x<3\), the range is \(-1<f(x)\le9\), or \((-1,9]\).

Decide whether the inverse exists

Check horizontal lines on the allowed graph. If any reaches two points, the output cannot identify one starting input. A restriction to one side of a parabola’s vertex can make it one–one.

Reverse the rule

  1. Write \(y=f(x)\), then solve for the old input \(x\).
  2. Rename the old output as the inverse input. Use the original range as the inverse domain.
\[f^{-1}(x)=\frac{5-x}{2},\qquad -1<x\le9.\]

Check the pair \(f(2)=1\) and \(f^{-1}(1)=2\). The range of \(f^{-1}\) is \(-2\le y<3\).
revision.checks:
• Check which endpoints are reached.
  • Check that each attained output has one original input.
  • Keep the inverse input restriction with the formula.
revision.examTip: Show a pair of equal outputs to disprove one–one. When finding an inverse, write the rearranged equation before renaming the variable, and state its domain separately.

orig_functions_composite.description: Learn composite functions for Cambridge 9709 Pure 1. Work out fg and gf, find their allowed inputs and keep domain restrictions after simplifying.

sections.title: Which function acts first?
sections.label: Read the order
sections.intro: In the first lesson, \(f(x)=5-2x\) took \(2\) to \(1\). Now let \(g(x)=x+1\) for all real \(x\). Start at \(1\), add \(1\) using \(g\), then put the result into \(f\). You have found \(fg(1)\).

blocks.html: Read \(fg(x)\) as \(f(g(x))\). Start with the function next to the input. Its output becomes the input of the second function. The notation \((f\circ g)(x)\) means the same thing. This calculation needs both steps to be defined at the chosen input.
Writing \(f(1)g(1)\) multiplies two separate outputs, \(3\times2=6\). For \(fg(1)\), pass the output \(2\) from \(g\) into \(f\), which gives \(1\).

blocks.prompt: Let \(p(x)=2x+3\) and \(q(x)=x-4\) for all real \(x\). Find \(pq(6)\).
blocks.hint: Find \(q(6)\) first. Use that result as the input of \(p\).

retry.feedback: Starting with \(p\) gives \(qp(6)\). In \(pq(6)\), \(q\) acts first, so start by subtracting \(4\).
You multiplied \(p(6)\) by \(q(6)\). Feed \(q(6)=2\) into \(p\) instead.

sections.title: How do I build the formula in either order?
sections.label: Build both formulae
sections.intro: Work with \(x\) instead of a single number. Write the outside rule with an empty input, then put the whole inside expression into that space.

blocks.html: In \(f(g(x))\), substitute the whole \(g(x)\) wherever the input occurs in \(f\). Use brackets before expanding. To find \(gf(x)\), switch which rule receives the substitution.
Start a written solution with \(fg(x)=f(g(x))\) to show the order. If the same rule is used twice, \(ff(x)=f(f(x))\). To square one output, write \([f(x)]^2\).

blocks.prompt: Let \(a(x)=x^2-3x\) and \(b(x)=2x+1\) for all real \(x\). Give the right-hand side of \(ab(x)\). Either expanded or bracketed form is fine.
blocks.hint: Put \(2x+1\) in both input positions of \(a\): the squared term and the term multiplied by \(-3\).

retry.feedback: You replaced the input in the square. Replace the second \(x\) in \(-3x\) with \(2x+1\) as well.
This applies \(a\) first and gives \(ba(x)\). For \(ab(x)\), apply \(b\) first.

blocks.prompt: For those same rules, \(a(x)=x^2-3x\) and \(b(x)=2x+1\), give the right-hand side of \(ba(x)\).
blocks.hint: This time \(x^2-3x\) goes into \(b\). Double the whole expression, then add \(1\).

retry.feedback: That is \(ab(x)\). For \(ba(x)\), the squared expression comes from \(a\), which acts first.

sections.title: Which inputs get through both functions?
sections.label: Check both domains
sections.intro: With \(g(x)=x+1\), an input of \(2\) gives \(g(2)=3\). The original function \(f(x)=5-2x\) has domain \(-2\le x<3\). Since it cannot take \(3\), the calculation of \(fg(2)\) stops there.

blocks.html:
1. Keep only inputs \(x\) that the inside function \(g\) accepts.
  2. Require the intermediate value \(g(x)\) to be in the domain of \(f\).
  3. Give the inputs that satisfy both conditions.

If asked whether \(fg\) can be formed for the functions as given, compare the whole range of \(g\) with the domain of \(f\). Every output of \(g\) must be accepted by \(f\). When only some inputs work, state the restriction on \(g\) explicitly.

blocks.prompt: Let \(p(t)=t^2\) on \(0\le t<5\), and \(q(x)=9-2x\) on \(-1\le x\le4\). Restrict \(q\) to the inputs that give a value for \(pq(x)\). Give that complete interval.
blocks.hint: Solve \(0\le9-2x<5\). Then take the overlap with \(-1\le x\le4\).
blocks.solution: The outside rule requires \(2<x\le\tfrac92\). The inside rule only takes \(x\le4\), so the allowed inputs are \(2<x\le4\), or \((2,4]\).

retry.feedback: You found when the outside rule accepts \(q(x)\). The original rule \(q\) also requires \(x\le4\).
These are all the inputs of \(q\). Keep only those whose outputs satisfy \(0\le q(x)<5\).
At \(x=2\), \(q(x)=5\). The outside rule excludes \(5\), so the lower endpoint is open.

blocks.prompt: Use \(q(x)=9-2x\) on its whole stated domain \(-1\le x\le4\). Give its largest output to show why \(pq\) cannot be formed on that whole domain.
blocks.hint: The line decreases. Which included input gives its largest output?
blocks.solution: At \(x=-1\), \(q(-1)=11\). This output is outside the interval \([0,5)\) accepted by \(p\).

retry.feedback: That is the input that gives the maximum. Substitute it into \(9-2x\) to get the output.
\(q(4)=1\) is the smallest output. Use the left-hand endpoint for the maximum.

sections.title: What if the outside rule contains a square root?
sections.label: Keep both branches
sections.intro: Let \(q(x)=x^2+3\) on \(-4\le x<3\). If the outside rule is \(p(t)=\sqrt{t-7}\), it only accepts values \(t\ge7\). Look for both parts of the graph of \(q\) at or above \(7\).

blocks.html: Write the condition on the inside output first. Here \(q(x)\ge7\) gives a quadratic inequality in \(x\). Solve it before applying the original bounds on \(x\).
\(x^2\ge4\) has two branches. For example, \(x=-3\) gives \(q(-3)=12\), which the outside root accepts. A radicand of zero is also allowed.

blocks.prompt: Let \(p(t)=\sqrt{t-13}\) for \(t\ge13\) and \(q(x)=x^2+4\) for \(-5\le x<4\). Give every input for which \(pq(x)\) is defined.
blocks.hint: Require \(x^2+4\ge13\). Take both branches of that inequality and keep their portions inside \([-5,4)\).
blocks.solution: \(x^2\ge9\) gives \(x\le-3\) or \(x\ge3\). With the stated domain of \(q\), the answer is \([-5,-3]\cup[3,4)\). In inequality notation, write \(-5\le x\le-3\) or \(3\le x<4\).

retry.feedback: This is the positive branch. Values with \(x\le-3\) can also have \(x^2\ge9\). Keep the part from \(-5\) to \(-3\).
This is the negative branch. The squared input is also at least \(9\) from \(3\) up to \(4\), excluding \(4\).
At \(x=-3\) and \(x=3\), the radicand is zero. Include both points.
Both square-root boundaries are included. The inside rule excludes \(x=4\), so use an open endpoint there.

sections.title: Can simplification bring back a forbidden input?
sections.label: Keep original exclusions
sections.intro: The graph below comes from composing two fractions. The rule simplifies to \(x-3\), but the inside fraction is undefined at \(3\). The hollow point is part of the final answer.

blocks.html: Write the exclusions from the two original steps before simplifying. Keep them alongside the resulting rule, even if a denominator disappears.

blocks.title: A link to inverses
blocks.html: When two rules undo each other, their composite gives back its input. For the \(f\) from the first lesson, \(f^{-1}(f(x))=x\) for \(-2\le x<3\). In the reverse order, \(f(f^{-1}(x))=x\) for \(-1<x\le9\). Both expressions are \(x\), with different allowed inputs.

blocks.prompt: Let \(p(t)=\dfrac4{t+1}\) for \(t\ne-1\), and \(q(x)=\dfrac2x\) for \(x\ne0\). Write \(pq(x)\) as one fraction. Enter the numerator and denominator separated by a semicolon.
blocks.hint: Start with \(\dfrac4{2/x+1}\). Write the denominator over a common denominator before simplifying.
blocks.solution: \(pq(x)=\dfrac4{2/x+1}=\dfrac{4x}{x+2}\). Enter 4x ; x + 2. You will account for both exclusions in the next check.

field.label: Complete domain of the fraction composite

blocks.prompt: For the same \(p(t)=\dfrac4{t+1}\) and \(q(x)=\dfrac2x\), give the full domain of \(pq\). You can join the exclusions with and.
blocks.hint: Keep \(x\ne0\), then also solve \(\dfrac2x\ne-1\).
blocks.solution: \(x=0\) is forbidden by \(q\). Also, \(q(-2)=-1\), which is forbidden by \(p\). So \(x\ne0\) and \(x\ne-2\). In interval notation this is \((-\infty,-2)\cup(-2,0)\cup(0,\infty)\).

retry.feedback: The finished denominator excludes \(-2\). Keep \(x=0\) out as well, because the original fraction \(q\) cannot take it.
You kept \(x=0\) out. Now check \(x=-2\): it gives \(q(-2)=-1\), where \(p\) is undefined.
Both exclusions must hold at the same time. Join \(x\ne-2\) and \(x\ne0\) with the word and.

sections.title: How can I recover a missing function?
sections.label: Recover a missing rule
sections.intro: If one rule and the composite are known, use the order of the composition to see what can be recovered. The missing rule may be on the inside or the outside.

blocks.html: If the outside rule is reversible on the relevant outputs, undo it to find the inside rule. If the inside rule is known, name its output \(t\) and rewrite the composite in terms of \(t\).

blocks.prompt: For all real \(x\), \(pq(x)=4x^2-6x+9\). The outside rule is \(p(t)=2t+7\) for real \(t\). Find the right-hand side of \(q(x)\).
blocks.hint: Set \(2q(x)+7\) equal to the given composite. Subtract \(7\), then divide by \(2\).
blocks.solution: \(2q(x)=4x^2-6x+2\), so \(q(x)=2x^2-3x+1\). Doubling this rule and adding \(7\) gives the required composite.

retry.feedback: You have found \(2q(x)\). Divide every term by \(2\) to obtain \(q(x)\).

blocks.html: A formula recovered for the outside function is justified only where the inside rule actually sends its inputs. State this interval with your formula.

blocks.prompt: Let \(g(x)=2x+1\) for \(x\ge0\), and suppose \(h(g(x))=6x-1\) throughout that interval. Find the right-hand side of \(h(x)\) on the inputs reached by \(g\).
blocks.hint: Let \(t=2x+1\), so \(x=\dfrac{t-1}{2}\). Substitute into \(6x-1\), then use \(x\) to denote the input of \(h\).
blocks.solution: \(h(t)=6\left(\dfrac{t-1}{2}\right)-1=3t-4\). Thus \(h(x)=3x-4\) for the inputs reached by \(g\).

retry.feedback: That formula takes the original input of \(g\). The input of \(h\) is \(2x+1\), so express the result in terms of this new input.

field.label: Inputs for which h is determined

blocks.prompt: For the same \(g(x)=2x+1\) on \(x\ge0\), give all inputs of \(h\) for which the composite determines its rule.
blocks.hint: Find the range of \(g\). It starts at \(g(0)\).
blocks.solution: Since \(g(0)=1\) and \(g\) increases, every value from \(1\) upwards is reached. The rule for \(h(x)\) is determined for \(x\ge1\).

retry.feedback: That is the domain of \(g\). The formula for \(h\) is determined on the outputs of \(g\), starting at \(1\).

examples.title: Follow the number through the two rules
examples.question: For \(f(x)=5-2x\), \(-2\le x<3\), and \(g(x)=x+1\), \(x\in\mathbb R\), find \(fg(1)\) and \(gf(1)\).
solution: For \(fg(1)\), start with \(g(1)=2\). The value \(2\) is allowed in \(f\), so \(fg(1)=f(2)=1\).
For \(gf(1)\), start with \(f(1)=3\). Now \(3\) goes into \(g\), which accepts every real input. So \(gf(1)=g(3)=4\).

examples.title: Replace the number with x
examples.question: Using the same \(f(x)=5-2x\) and \(g(x)=x+1\), find the two composite formulae wherever they are defined.
solution:
For \(fg\), the inside rule gives \(x+1\). Replace the input of \(f\) with \(x+1\).

\[fg(x)=5-2(x+1)=3-2x.\]

For \(gf\), the inside rule gives \(5-2x\). The outside rule \(g\) adds \(1\).

\[gf(x)=(5-2x)+1=6-2x.\]
At \(x=1\), the formulae give \(1\) and \(4\), matching the two calculations in the previous section. Now check which other inputs are allowed.

examples.title: Replace every input in a quadratic rule
examples.question: Let \(a(x)=x^2+2x\) and \(b(x)=x-3\) on the real numbers. Find \(ab(x)\) and \(ba(x)\).
solution:
Write the outside rule as \(a(t)=t^2+2t\). Both places marked \(t\) receive \(x-3\).

\[ab(x)=(x-3)^2+2(x-3).\]
Expand the square and the linear term to get \(ab(x)=x^2-4x+3\).

With \(b\) on the outside, subtract \(3\) from the entire output of \(a\).

\[ba(x)=x^2+2x-3.\]

examples.title: Find the inputs that pass both checks
examples.question: For \(f(x)=5-2x\) on \([-2,3)\) and \(g(x)=x+1\) on \(\mathbb R\), which inputs work in \(fg\)? Which work in \(gf\)?
solution:
For \(fg\), \(g\) can start at any real \(x\). The intermediate value \(x+1\) must belong to \([-2,3)\).

\[-2\le x+1<3.\]
Subtract \(1\) throughout. The inputs that work are \(-3\le x<2\), or \([-3,2)\). In particular, \(x=-3\) works and \(x=2\) does not.
For \(gf\), start with the given domain of \(f\), \([-2,3)\). Every output of \(f\) is real and \(g\) accepts every real number, so there is no further restriction.

examples.title: Find two intervals from one square root
examples.question: For \(p(t)=\sqrt{t-7}\) on \(t\ge7\), and \(q(x)=x^2+3\) on \(-4\le x<3\), find \(pq(x)\) and its domain.
solution: The outside rule needs \(q(x)\ge7\), so \(x^2+3\ge7\), or \(x^2\ge4\).
This is true when \(x\le-2\) or \(x\ge2\). The endpoints \(-2\) and \(2\) give a square root of zero, so both are allowed.
Restrict both branches to the stated interval \([-4,3)\). The composite is \(pq(x)=\sqrt{x^2-4}\) on \([-4,-2]\cup[2,3)\).

examples.title: A straight line with one missing point
examples.question: Find \(pq(x)\) when \(p(t)=\dfrac5{t-2}\), \(t\ne2\), and \(q(x)=2+\dfrac5{x-3}\), \(x\ne3\). State the domain.
solution: First record \(x\ne3\) from \(q\). For every allowed \(x\), the fraction in \(q\) is non-zero. So its output never equals \(2\) and the outside rule takes it.

Substitute the output of \(q\) into \(p\).

\[pq(x)=\dfrac5{q(x)-2}=\dfrac5{5/(x-3)}=x-3.\]
The resulting rule is \(x-3\) for \(x\ne3\). At \(x=3\) the first step still has no value, so the point \((3,0)\) is absent.

examples.title: Undo the outside function
examples.question: Let \(a(t)=3t-5\) for real \(t\), and let \(ab(x)=6x^2-9x+7\) for real \(x\). Find \(b(x)\).
solution: The outside rule acts on \(b(x)\). That makes the equation \(3b(x)-5=6x^2-9x+7\).

Add \(5\) to both sides and divide every term by \(3\).

\[b(x)=2x^2-3x+4.\]
Putting this into \(3b(x)-5\) gives \(6x^2-9x+7\), as required.

examples.title: Find the outside rule on the inputs it receives
examples.question: Let \(q(x)=x+4\) for \(x\ge-2\), and suppose \(p(q(x))=x^2+3x\) throughout that interval. Find the rule for \(p\) wherever it is determined.
solution: The input of \(p\) is \(t=q(x)=x+4\). Since \(x\ge-2\), we know that \(t\ge2\). Express the old input as \(x=t-4\).

Substitute \(t-4\) into the given composite and simplify.

\[p(t)=(t-4)^2+3(t-4)=t^2-5t+4.\]
This determines \(p(t)\) for \(t\ge2\). Smaller values of \(t\) are never reached by the stated \(q\), so the composite gives no information about them.

glossary.definition: Two functions used in order, with the first output fed into the second function.
The rule applied first. In \(fg(x)=f(g(x))\), this is \(g\).
The rule that takes the first output as its input. In \(fg(x)\), this is \(f\).
The original inputs that pass through both rules.
A condition that limits which inputs a function accepts.

revision.body:
Read the order

\(fg(x)=f(g(x))\). Apply \(g\) first, then feed its output into \(f\). Put the full inside expression into every input position.

For \(f(x)=5-2x\) on \([-2,3)\) and \(g(x)=x+1\) on \(\mathbb R\), the two orders give different results at \(x=1\).

Check both domains

Check that \(x\) is allowed in \(g\) and \(g(x)\) is allowed in \(f\). For all of \(g\)'s domain to work, its whole range must lie inside the domain of \(f\).

In the example above, solve \(-2\le x+1<3\). The domain of the restricted composite \(fg\) is \([-3,2)\).

Keep exclusions and recover rules

Record square-root conditions and both sets of denominator restrictions before simplifying. To recover an inside rule, undo the outside rule. To recover an outside rule, express the composite in terms of the first output and state where it is reached.
revision.checks:
• Identify which function acts first.
  • Check endpoints and both branches of an inequality.
  • Keep every exclusion alongside the simplified rule.
revision.examTip: Show the intermediate condition, such as \(g(x)\ge7\), before solving for \(x\). In a question about the full stated domain, one forbidden output is enough to show that the whole domain cannot work.
